source.title: Some unsolved problems in number theory

accepted.question_text: Do there exist natural numbers x1, x2, x3, x4, x5, and z such that x1^6 + x2^6 + x3^6 + x4^6 + x5^6 = z^6? In other words, is it possible for the sum of five sixth powers of natural numbers to equal another sixth power?

evidence.quote: What about sixth powers? Is it possible for the sum of five sixth powers to equal another sixth power?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a rectangular box with positive integer side lengths x, y, and z such that all three face diagonals, namely sqrt(x^2 + y^2), sqrt(x^2 + z^2), and sqrt(y^2 + z^2), and also the main space diagonal sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2), are all integers?

evidence.quote: Is it possible for all of the numbers x, y, z, √x2 + y2 + z2, √x2 + y2, √x2 + z2, and√y2 + z2 to be integers? In other words, does there exist a box with sides of integer length whose three face diagonals and main diagonal all have integer length as well?

accepted.question_text: Fix a rational number p/q with q odd. Starting from p/q, repeatedly choose the smallest odd integer n1 such that 1/n1 < p/q, then the smallest odd integer n2 such that 1/n1 + 1/n2 < p/q, then continue in the same way, always restricting the denominators to odd integers. Must this specific odd-denominator greedy unit-fraction procedure always terminate after finitely many steps?

evidence.quote: What if you restrict all the denominators in the procedure to be odd? In other words, you start with a fraction p/q where q is odd, and then find the smallest odd number n1 such that 1/n1 < p/q, and then the smallest odd number n2 such that 1/n1 + 1/n2 < p/q , and so on. Will this procedure always stop after a finite number of steps?

(Notice that this is not the same as asking whether it is possible to express p/q as the sum of unit fractions with odd denominator. Instead, the question is whether this particular method for finding such a sum will always work.)

accepted.question_text: Does there exist an odd perfect number, meaning a positive odd integer that is equal to the sum of its positive divisors other than itself?

evidence.quote: 16. Two unsolved problems about perfect numbers, which we mentioned in class: 1. Does there exist an odd perfect number?

accepted.question_text: Are there infinitely many even perfect numbers, meaning positive even integers that are equal to the sum of their positive divisors other than themselves?

evidence.quote: 16. Two unsolved problems about perfect numbers, which we mentioned in class: ... 2. Do there exist infinitely many even perfect numbers?

accepted.question_text: Let π(x) denote the number of prime numbers less than or equal to x, and let li(x) = ∫_0^x 1/log t dt. Does there exist a constant C such that for every real number x, the error |π(x) - li(x)| is less than C√x log x?

evidence.quote: Namely, can one find a constant C such that for every real number x, the difference between π(x) and ∫ x 0 1/log t dt is less than C√x log x?

accepted.question_text: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that determines the prime factorization of every positive integer N, where polynomial time means that if d is the number of decimal digits of N then the algorithm uses at most C d^k additions and multiplications for some fixed constants C and k independent of N?

evidence.quote: Does such an algorithm exist?

An algorithm for determining the prime factorization of a number N is said to be a polynomial-time algorithm if for every number N, the algorithm accomplishes its task without having to do more than Cd^k additions and multiplications, where d is the number of digits in the number N, and C and k are fixed constants (independent of N).

accepted.question_text: Starting from a positive integer n, repeatedly replace n by n/2 when n is even and by 3n + 1 when n is odd. Does there exist any starting number for which this iteration never eventually reaches 1?

evidence.quote: Starting with any given number n, do the following: if n is even, divide it by 2; but if n is odd, multiply it by 3 and add 1. Now take the result and repeat the procedure.
Does there exist any number for which the procedure does not eventually lead to 1?

accepted.question_text: Given any polynomial equation with integer coefficients in finitely many unknowns x1, x2, ..., xn, is there an algorithm that decides whether the equation has a solution in rational numbers x1, x2, ..., xn, and that always settles the question after finitely many steps for every such polynomial?

evidence.quote: Suppose you are given a polynomial equation, with integer coefficients, in n unknown variables x1, x2, x3, . . . , xn. ... Is there an algorithm for deciding whether there exist rational numbers x1, x2, . . . x n which satisfy the equation?
The desired algorithm must work for every possible polynomial in the sense that it will settle the question in a finite number of steps.

accepted.question_text: Do the digits in the decimal expansion of π behave without any hidden pattern in the sense that every finite digit string occurs with the expected frequency, so that no digit block appears systematically more or less often than another?

evidence.quote: No one has yet been able to determine any pattern in the digits of the decimal expansion of π, or to prove that there is no pattern.

one way to interpret the absence of a pattern in the digits would be to say that any combination of digits (such as 6574) occurs no more or less frequently in the decimal expansion of π than any other combination. No result along these lines is currently known.

accepted.question_text: Is exactly 10% of the digits in the decimal expansion of π equal to 7, in the limiting frequency sense suggested by the source?

evidence.quote: For example, it is not known whether 10% of the digits in the decimal expansion of π are sevens.

accepted.question_text: Is π/e a rational number? Equivalently, is π a rational multiple of e?

evidence.quote: 22. Is π/e a rational number? It is known that both π and e are irrational, but it is not known whether π is a rational multiple of e.

accepted.question_text: Is π + e a rational number?

evidence.quote: Nor is it known whether π + e or π ·e are rational numbers.
Nor is it known whether π + e or π ·e are rational numbers.

accepted.question_text: Is there an algorithm that computes the first n digits of the decimal expansion of √2 using an amount of work proportional to n, where the amount of work is measured by the total number of additions and multiplications used to obtain those digits?

evidence.quote: Can one find an algorithm which computes the first n digits in the decimal expansion of √2 by doing an amount of work which is proportional to n?
You can interpret “amount of work” to mean the total number of additions and multiplications required to find the digits.

accepted.question_text: Is the infinite series 1 + 1/2^5 + 1/3^5 + ... irrational? Equivalently, if ζ(5) denotes the sum of 1/n^5 over all positive integers n, is ζ(5) irrational?

evidence.quote: That raises the question: is the sum of the series 1 + 1/25 + 1/35 + . . . an irrational number?
